reason: I did not trust the verifier's WebFetch summary, which garbled the poem's end twice (one pass called the last twelve lines the eight beginning "The heart can push the sea and land", another said the poem concludes at "And let the face of God shine through"). So I pulled the primary text myself: curl of https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/109/pg109.txt, 1612 lines, and read the raw bytes around line 340. The closing block is exactly twelve lines, set off by a blank line after "God, I can push the grass apart / And lay my finger on Thy heart!", and it runs: "The world stands out on either side / No wider than the heart is wide; / Above the world is stretched the sky,-- / No higher than the soul is high. / The heart can push the sea and land / Farther away on either hand; / The soul can split the sky in two, / And let the face of God shine through. / But East and West will pinch the heart / That can not keep them pushed apart; / And he whose soul is flat--the sky / Will cave in on him by and by." The proposal takes its first four, character for character, including the semicolon after "wide", the comma before the dash after "sky", and the full stop after "high". The plain-text file renders the dash as two hyphens, which is Gutenberg's ASCII convention; the HTML edition of the same ebook prints it as an em dash, which is what the proposal has, so the punctuation is the edition's and not minted. VERSE RULE: four lines, slash with a space each side, the poem's own capitals at each line head (The, No, Above, No), never run together as prose. Correct. The em dash inside the quotation is not a rule breach: rule 5 bans the em dash in the SOURCE and the NOTE only, and the carry-in 05-poet-12 (Hikmet, "like a squirrel, for example-") already ships one inside a quotation. ATTRIBUTION: not a trap. Renascence is Millay's, and nothing on the misattribution list touches it; the speaker is the poem's own "I" and not a named character, so no parenthetical speaker is owed. GATES: shipped.js returns shipped [], near [], Millay at 0 for the year, cap 3, not banned; and she appears once in the whole month's 54 candidates, so rule 8 is clean. SCOPE: a poem first printed in The Lyric Year in 1912 and collected in 1917, long before 1999, not scripture, film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory. Publishable with nothing to warn of. SOURCE LINE: 133 characters, inside the cap, leads with the author's name, carries no dash, no straight double quote. TAG Poetry is the form of the work. ONE NON-FATAL REMARK. The locator reads "the closing verse paragraph, lines 1 to 4", and "lines 1 to 4" standing next to a poem title invites the reader to think of the poem's own opening ("All I could see from where I stood"). The facts are right, only the phrasing is loose; "the closing twelve lines, the first four" would remove the ambiguity and still fit the 140. The 1917 Mitchell Kennerley imprint is not printed in the Gutenberg file, which names no publisher, but it is the standard first edition of that title and I found nothing contradicting it.
